doc.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Bassist Jeff Castleman on playing with Bellson
summary: Brown reads Castleman's praise of Bellson as a kind person; Bellson says the same of working with him.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: I’m going to read another quote. This one – of course we’re going back to the book of Duke – this one’s The World of Duke Ellington, Stanley Dance. This is an interview with – well, let’s see if you recognize who this is from. I’ll read it – I’ll go ahead and identify it. You know who it is: Jeff Castleman.

Yeah, Stanley Dance, but I’m going to read an interview that was conducted with Jeff Castleman. This is what Jeff says: “I really enjoy playing with Louis.” He didn’t call you Louie. He called you Louis Bellson. “I like the atmosphere in a small group better, but Louis made the big band relaxed for me. He played so well that I never worried.” It sounds like you and Duke. “He’s a nice guy, an angel, and it was a wonderful experience. He opened my eyes to how nice the business could be, that you could be a nice guy and play well too. I learned so much from him that I progressed a lot further than I would have otherwise.” So here again your influence, the extra-musical influence.

Right back I’d say the same thing. I found him easy to work with. He had the right attitude. We were playing great music. We worked together. You can’t beat that combination, working together. If you have a problem, you solve it right there. Don’t let it ride over and be a part of your ugly side. Do what you have to do, and do it the best you can. That’s what he did. He was a good bass player too. I saw him not too long ago. They had a get-together of all the people that worked with Duke. Singers – Herb Jeffries was there. 93 years old and still singing – still got the voice.
